report:
Conclusion: The evidence is mixed, so a confident “yes” is not well supported. Some meta-analyses report a statistically significant reduction in muscle pain intensity with CoQ10, while others find no convincing benefit, and major health authorities remain skeptical.

Supporting evidence:
- A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Nutritional Science pooled 7 RCTs (389 patients) and found an overall significant reduction in muscle pain intensity with CoQ10 versus control in patients with existing statin-induced myopathy (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-nutritional-science/article/effects-of-coenzyme-q10-supplementation-on-myopathy-in-statintreated-patients-a-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/21158F64C8D162585D71D5616B075E05).
- A 2018 AHA meta-analysis (Qu et al.) concluded that CoQ10 did not show a significant benefit for statin-induced myopathy, noting conflicting results across trials (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.118.009835).
- Harvard Health, summarizing a review of 431 reports, states there is no convincing evidence that CoQ10 prevents statin-related muscle pain, though a short trial is reasonable given low risk (https://www.health.harvard.edu/heart-health/coq10-for-muscle-aches).
- A PMC review similarly notes the clinical benefit of CoQ10 supplementation remains unproven (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6054172/).

Bottom line: CoQ10 may help some individuals, but the overall evidence is inconsistent; it is not reliably proven to relieve statin-associated muscle discomfort.
